claim: Mental imagery is among the most ubiquitous human experiences in daily life.
source: The subjective inner experience of mental imagery is among the most ubiquitous human experiences in daily life.
evidence: This is a general statement about mental imagery presented in the abstract without specific experimental data or citations in this sentence.

claim: People spend more than one-quarter of their lifetime engaged in speech mental imagery experiences.
source: Speech mental imagery is among the most pervasive human experiences, and it has been estimated that people spend more than one-quarter of their lifetime engaged in such inner experiences (Heavey and Hurlburt, 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Heavey and Hurlburt, 2008.

claim: Many fMRI studies have reported distributed neural networks involving the left pars opercularis in the inferior frontal cortex (Broca's area) that can be activated by speech mental imagery.
source: Many functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) studies have reported distributed neural networks involving the left pars opercularis in the inferior frontal cortex (Broca's area) (Aleman et al., 2005; Kleber et al., 2007; Papoutsi et al., 2009; Koelsch et al., 2009; Price, 2012; Tian et al., 2016), the premotor cortex (Price, 2012; Kleber et al., 2007; Koelsch et al., 2009; Tian et al., 2016; Aleman et al., 2005), the inferior parietal lobe (Kleber et al., 2007; Tian et al., 2016), the middle frontal cortex (Tian et al., 2016), the anterior part of the insula (Koelsch et al., 2009; Tian et al., 2016; Aleman et al., 2005; Ackermann and Riecker, 2004), and the superior temporal gyrus (Aleman et al., 2005) that can be activated by speech mental imagery.
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to previous fMRI studies.

claim: The temporal resolution of fMRI technique has limited investigation of the neural dynamics of speech mental imagery.
source: However, limited by the temporal resolution of the fMRI technique, the neural dynamics of speech mental imagery have been mostly overlooked.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of fMRI based on established knowledge about the technique's temporal resolution.

claim: Neuronal information processing is shaped by multiscale oscillatory activity.
source: Neuronal information processing is shaped by multiscale oscillatory activity (Buzsáki and Draguhn, 2004), in which subjective experience in consciousness involves ongoing neural dynamics on the time scale of hundreds of milliseconds (Dehaene and Changeux, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Buzsáki and Draguhn, 2004 and Dehaene and Changeux, 2011.

claim: Subjective experience in consciousness involves ongoing neural dynamics on the time scale of hundreds of milliseconds.
source: Neuronal information processing is shaped by multiscale oscillatory activity (Buzsáki and Draguhn, 2004), in which subjective experience in consciousness involves ongoing neural dynamics on the time scale of hundreds of milliseconds (Dehaene and Changeux, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Dehaene and Changeux, 2011.

claim: Preliminary MEG studies have shown that the modulatory effect of imagined speech on the amplitude of event-related responses to a subsequent auditory stimulus with matched pitch and/or content occurs as early as 100 to 200 ms.
source: Preliminary magnetoencephalography (MEG) studies have shown that the modulatory effect of imagined speech on the amplitude of event-related responses to a subsequent auditory stimulus with matched pitch and/or content occurs as early as 100 to 200 ms (Tian and Poeppel, 2013; Tian and Poeppel, 2015; Ylinen et al., 2015), and in an electroencephalogram (EEG) study, N1 suppression was observed when a matched phoneme was generated covertly before an audible phoneme was presented (Whitford et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous MEG studies.

claim: N1 suppression was observed in an EEG study when a matched phoneme was generated covertly before an audible phoneme was presented.
source: Preliminary magnetoencephalography (MEG) studies have shown that the modulatory effect of imagined speech on the amplitude of event-related responses to a subsequent auditory stimulus with matched pitch and/or content occurs as early as 100 to 200 ms (Tian and Poeppel, 2013; Tian and Poeppel, 2015; Ylinen et al., 2015), and in an electroencephalogram (EEG) study, N1 suppression was observed when a matched phoneme was generated covertly before an audible phoneme was presented (Whitford et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Whitford et al., 2017.

claim: Tian et al. (2018) demonstrated the involvement of the sensory-driven cortex (i.e. the auditory cortex) in the early-stage interaction of speech imagery and perception.
source: Recently, Tian et al. (2018) examined the influence of imagined speech on the perceived loudness of a subsequent syllable and demonstrated the involvement of the sensory-driven cortex (i.e. the auditory cortex) in the early-stage interaction of speech imagery and perception.
evidence: Supported by citation to Tian et al., 2018.

claim: In the adaptation paradigm, the neural pathway of top-down mental imagery cannot be disentangled from the bottom-up perception.
source: These neurophysiological findings implicate the early involvement of sensory-related neural substrates in the process of speech mental imagery, while in the adaptation paradigm, the neural pathway of top-down mental imagery cannot be disentangled from the bottom-up perception.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the limitations of the adaptation paradigm described in the context.

claim: Frequency-tagging has been used to characterize higher-level processes such as music rhythmic perception.
source: Recently, frequency-tagging has been used to characterize higher-lever processes such as music rhythmic perception (Nozaradan et al., 2011; Tal et al., 2017; Lenc et al., 2018; Nozaradan et al., 2018) and speech linguistic construction (Ding et al., 2016; Sheng et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies using frequency-tagging.

claim: Frequency-tagging has been used to characterize speech linguistic construction.
source: Recently, frequency-tagging has been used to characterize higher-lever processes such as music rhythmic perception (Nozaradan et al., 2011; Tal et al., 2017; Lenc et al., 2018; Nozaradan et al., 2018) and speech linguistic construction (Ding et al., 2016; Sheng et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Ding et al., 2016 and Sheng et al., 2019.

claim: Nozaradan et al. (2011) found spectral responses not only to the beat stimulation but also to the imagined meters of the beat when musicians imagined a binary/ternary meter while listening to a constant beat.
source: For example, Nozaradan et al. (2011) asked eight musicians to imagine a binary/ternary meter when listening to a constant beat and found spectral responses not only to the beat stimulation but also to the imagined meters of this beat.
evidence: Supported by citation to Nozaradan et al., 2011.

claim: Ding et al. (2016) reported cortical responses to internally constructed linguistic structures such as words, phrases and sentences at different frequencies during the comprehension of connected speech.
source: Ding et al. (2016) reported cortical responses to internally constructed linguistic structures such as words, phrases and sentences at different frequencies during the comprehension of connected speech.
evidence: Supported by citation to Ding et al., 2016.

claim: The study manipulated the imagery-rate frequency to 0.8 Hz.
source: In this way, we are able to directly track the neural processing time scales of speech mental imagery in the frequency domain (in our experiment, we manipulated the imagery-rate frequency to 0.8 Hz).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental design.

claim: The study used MEG source estimation method to localize the neural underpinnings of the isolated processes of speech imagery independent of the bottom-up auditory perception.
source: Furthermore, we used the MEG source estimation method to localize the neural underpinnings of the isolated processes of speech imagery independent of the bottom-up auditory perception and confirmed the localization of the neural sources by intracranial stereotactic electroencephalogram (sEEG) recordings.
evidence: This describes the methodology used in the study.

claim: The study confirmed the localization of neural sources by intracranial stereotactic electroencephalogram (sEEG) recordings.
source: Furthermore, we used the MEG source estimation method to localize the neural underpinnings of the isolated processes of speech imagery independent of the bottom-up auditory perception and confirmed the localization of the neural sources by intracranial stereotactic electroencephalogram (sEEG) recordings.
evidence: This describes the methodology used in the study.

claim: The spectral peaks were significant at the frequency of 0.8 Hz when subjects were performing the mental imagery task.
source: As a result, when the subjects were performing the task, the spectral peaks were significant at the frequency of 0.8 Hz, corresponding to the grouping-rate rhythm of the mental imagery (t19 = 5.33, p=4.2 × 10−4, Cohen's d = 1.19, one-tailed paired t test, false discovery rate [FDR] corrected), and at the frequency of 4 Hz, corresponding to the rate of the auditory stimuli (t19 = 18.45, corrected p=3.0 × 10−12, Cohen's d = 4.13) (Figure 1b).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data and shown in Figure 1b.

claim: The spectral peaks were significant at the frequency of 4 Hz when subjects were performing the mental imagery task.
source: As a result, when the subjects were performing the task, the spectral peaks were significant at the frequency of 0.8 Hz, corresponding to the grouping-rate rhythm of the mental imagery (t19 = 5.33, p=4.2 × 10−4, Cohen's d = 1.19, one-tailed paired t test, false discovery rate [FDR] corrected), and at the frequency of 4 Hz, corresponding to the rate of the auditory stimuli (t19 = 18.45, corrected p=3.0 × 10−12, Cohen's d = 4.13) (Figure 1b).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data and shown in Figure 1b.

claim: An additional harmonic peak at 1.6 Hz was found at the significance level of 0.05.
source: An additional harmonic peak at 1.6 Hz was found at the significance level of 0.05 (t19 = 3.18, corrected p=0.04, Cohen's d = 0.96).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: No significant peaks were observed at the harmonic frequencies of 2.4 Hz.
source: No significant peaks were observed at the harmonic frequencies of 2.4 Hz (t19 = 2.46, corrected p=0.10, Cohen's d = 0.55) and 3.2 Hz (t19 = 2.75, corrected p=0.07, marginally significant, Cohen's d = 0.62).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: Under the control (baseline) condition, a significant peak was observed only at the stimulus-rate frequency of 4 Hz.
source: In contrast, under the control (baseline) condition, in which the participant received identical auditory stimuli without the imagery task, a significant peak was observed only at the stimulus-rate frequency of 4 Hz (t19 = 14.23, corrected p=3.1 × 10−10, Cohen's d = 3.18).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: The averaged power over the sensors in the right hemisphere was significantly stronger than that in the left hemisphere at 4 Hz under the mental imagery condition.
source: Specifically, the two-tailed paired t test showed that the averaged power over the sensors in the right hemisphere was significantly stronger than that in the left hemisphere at 4 Hz under both the mental imagery condition (t19 = 3.78, p=0.001, Cohen's d = 0.84) and the baseline condition (t19 = 3.21, p=0.004, Cohen's d = 0.72) but not at the imagery-rate frequency of 0.8 Hz under the mental imagery condition (t19 = 0.34, p=0.72, Cohen's d = 0.08).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: The averaged power over the sensors in the right hemisphere was significantly stronger than that in the left hemisphere at 4 Hz under the baseline condition.
source: Specifically, the two-tailed paired t test showed that the averaged power over the sensors in the right hemisphere was significantly stronger than that in the left hemisphere at 4 Hz under both the mental imagery condition (t19 = 3.78, p=0.001, Cohen's d = 0.84) and the baseline condition (t19 = 3.21, p=0.004, Cohen's d = 0.72) but not at the imagery-rate frequency of 0.8 Hz under the mental imagery condition (t19 = 0.34, p=0.72, Cohen's d = 0.08).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: There was no significant difference in averaged power between right and left hemispheres at the imagery-rate frequency of 0.8 Hz under the mental imagery condition.
source: Specifically, the two-tailed paired t test showed that the averaged power over the sensors in the right hemisphere was significantly stronger than that in the left hemisphere at 4 Hz under both the mental imagery condition (t19 = 3.78, p=0.001, Cohen's d = 0.84) and the baseline condition (t19 = 3.21, p=0.004, Cohen's d = 0.72) but not at the imagery-rate frequency of 0.8 Hz under the mental imagery condition (t19 = 0.34, p=0.72, Cohen's d = 0.08).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: The peak power at the imagery-rate frequency of 0.8 Hz when the participants induced rhythmic mental imagery was significantly larger than that under the baseline condition.
source: A two-tailed paired t test showed that the peak power at the imagery-rate frequency of 0.8 Hz when the participants induced rhythmic mental imagery was significantly larger than that under the baseline condition (t19 = 2.40, p=0.027, Cohen's d = 0.54).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data and shown in Figure 2a.

claim: No significant difference was observed between the two conditions at 4 Hz in peak power.
source: No significant difference was observed between the two conditions at 4 Hz (t19 = −0.30, p=0.764, Cohen's d = 0.07).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: The power of the neural responses at an imagery rate of 0.8 Hz was negatively correlated with that at a stimulus rate of 4 Hz when the participants induced the rhythmic mental imagery following the sound sequence.
source: Interestingly, the power of the neural responses at an imagery rate of 0.8 Hz was negatively correlated with that at a stimulus rate of 4 Hz when the participants induced the rhythmic mental imagery following the sound sequence (r = −0.68, p=0.001) but not when they passively listened to the auditory stimuli (r = −0.11, p=0.63) (Figure 2b).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis of experimental data and shown in Figure 2b.

claim: There was no significant correlation between the power at 0.8 Hz and 4 Hz when participants passively listened to the auditory stimuli.
source: Interestingly, the power of the neural responses at an imagery rate of 0.8 Hz was negatively correlated with that at a stimulus rate of 4 Hz when the participants induced the rhythmic mental imagery following the sound sequence (r = −0.68, p=0.001) but not when they passively listened to the auditory stimuli (r = −0.11, p=0.63) (Figure 2b).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis of experimental data and shown in Figure 2b.

claim: The left central-frontal lobe, including the pars opercularis part of the inferior frontal gyrus (operIFG), the inferior part of the precentral gyrus (PrG) and the postcentral gyrus (PoG), was significantly activated at the imagery-rate frequency of 0.8 Hz.
source: As a result, we found the following significant clusters activated at the imagery-rate frequency of 0.8 Hz (Figure 3, Table 1): (1) the left central-frontal lobe, including the pars opercularis part of the inferior frontal gyrus (operIFG), the inferior part of the precentral gyrus (PrG) and the postcentral gyrus (PoG), (2) the left inferior occipital gyrus (IOG) and (3) the right inferior parietal lobe (IPL), including the supramarginal gyrus (SMG) and the inferior part of the PoG (cluster level p<0.01, family-wise error [FWE] corrected with a voxel-level threshold of p<0.001).
evidence: Supported by MEG source estimation analysis and shown in Figure 3 and Table 1.

claim: The left inferior occipital gyrus (IOG) was significantly activated at the imagery-rate frequency of 0.8 Hz.
source: As a result, we found the following significant clusters activated at the imagery-rate frequency of 0.8 Hz (Figure 3, Table 1): (1) the left central-frontal lobe, including the pars opercularis part of the inferior frontal gyrus (operIFG), the inferior part of the precentral gyrus (PrG) and the postcentral gyrus (PoG), (2) the left inferior occipital gyrus (IOG) and (3) the right inferior parietal lobe (IPL), including the supramarginal gyrus (SMG) and the inferior part of the PoG (cluster level p<0.01, family-wise error [FWE] corrected with a voxel-level threshold of p<0.001).
evidence: Supported by MEG source estimation analysis and shown in Figure 3 and Table 1.

claim: The right inferior parietal lobe (IPL), including the supramarginal gyrus (SMG) and the inferior part of the PoG, was significantly activated at the imagery-rate frequency of 0.8 Hz.
source: As a result, we found the following significant clusters activated at the imagery-rate frequency of 0.8 Hz (Figure 3, Table 1): (1) the left central-frontal lobe, including the pars opercularis part of the inferior frontal gyrus (operIFG), the inferior part of the precentral gyrus (PrG) and the postcentral gyrus (PoG), (2) the left inferior occipital gyrus (IOG) and (3) the right inferior parietal lobe (IPL), including the supramarginal gyrus (SMG) and the inferior part of the PoG (cluster level p<0.01, family-wise error [FWE] corrected with a voxel-level threshold of p<0.001).
evidence: Supported by MEG source estimation analysis and shown in Figure 3 and Table 1.

claim: A more extensive brain network involving the bilateral Heschl's gyrus (HG), right middle temporal gyrus (MTG), left SMG, bilateral superior temporal gyrus (STG), bilateral PrG, bilateral PoG and bilateral insula (INS) was significantly activated at the stimulus-rate frequency of 4 Hz under both the mental imagery and the baseline conditions.
source: Regarding the stimulus-rate frequency of 4 Hz, a more extensive brain network involving the bilateral Heschl's gyrus (HG), right middle temporal gyrus (MTG), left SMG, bilateral superior temporal gyrus (STG), bilateral PrG, bilateral PoG and bilateral insula (INS) was significantly activated under both the mental imagery and the baseline conditions.
evidence: Supported by MEG source estimation analysis.

claim: The right middle frontal gyrus (MFG) was activated at 4 Hz under the mental imagery condition.
source: An additional region in the right middle frontal gyrus (MFG) was also activated at 4 Hz under the mental imagery condition.
evidence: Supported by MEG source estimation analysis.

claim: The neural responses in the left IOG at 0.8 Hz under the mental imagery condition were significantly stronger than those at 4 Hz under the mental imagery condition and at 4 Hz under the baseline condition.
source: The results showed that in the left hemisphere, the neural responses in the left IOG at 0.8 Hz under the mental imagery condition were significantly stronger than those at 4 Hz under the mental imagery condition and at 4 Hz under the baseline condition (both p<0.05).
evidence: Supported by post hoc comparisons with Bonferroni correction and shown in Figure 4.

claim: The neural activation at 4 Hz under the imagery and baseline conditions was stronger than that at 0.8 Hz under the imagery condition in the left HG.
source: In addition, the neural activation at 4 Hz under the imagery and baseline conditions was stronger than that at 0.8 Hz under the imagery condition in the left HG (p=0.058 and p<0.001, respectively), the left INS (p=0.012 and p<0.001, respectively) and the left SMG (p=0.032 and p<0.001, respectively).
evidence: Supported by post hoc comparisons with Bonferroni correction.

claim: The neural activation at 4 Hz under the imagery and baseline conditions was stronger than that at 0.8 Hz under the imagery condition in the left INS.
source: In addition, the neural activation at 4 Hz under the imagery and baseline conditions was stronger than that at 0.8 Hz under the imagery condition in the left HG (p=0.058 and p<0.001, respectively), the left INS (p=0.012 and p<0.001, respectively) and the left SMG (p=0.032 and p<0.001, respectively).
evidence: Supported by post hoc comparisons with Bonferroni correction.

claim: The neural activation at 4 Hz under the imagery and baseline conditions was stronger than that at 0.8 Hz under the imagery condition in the left SMG.
source: In addition, the neural activation at 4 Hz under the imagery and baseline conditions was stronger than that at 0.8 Hz under the imagery condition in the left HG (p=0.058 and p<0.001, respectively), the left INS (p=0.012 and p<0.001, respectively) and the left SMG (p=0.032 and p<0.001, respectively).
evidence: Supported by post hoc comparisons with Bonferroni correction.

claim: In the left STG, the activation amplitude at 4 Hz under the baseline condition was larger than that at 0.8 Hz under the imagery condition.
source: In the left STG, the activation amplitude at 4 Hz under the baseline condition was larger than that at 0.8 Hz under the imagery condition (p=0.006).
evidence: Supported by post hoc comparisons with Bonferroni correction.

claim: The activation observed at 4 Hz under the imagery and baseline conditions was stronger than that observed at 0.8 Hz under the imagery condition in the right HG.
source: In the right hemisphere, the activation observed at 4 Hz under the imagery and baseline conditions was stronger than that observed at 0.8 Hz under the imagery condition in most regions (right HG, both p<0.001; right STG, both p<0.001; right INS, both p=0.003; right PrG, p=0.029 and 0.016, respectively; right PoG, p=0.025 and 0.010, respectively; right MTG, p=0.010 and 0.005, respectively; all with Bonferroni correction), reflecting robust auditory neural representations of the 4 Hz sequence of sound stimuli.
evidence: Supported by post hoc comparisons with Bonferroni correction.

claim: The activation observed at 4 Hz under the imagery and baseline conditions was stronger than that observed at 0.8 Hz under the imagery condition in the right STG.
source: In the right hemisphere, the activation observed at 4 Hz under the imagery and baseline conditions was stronger than that observed at 0.8 Hz under the imagery condition in most regions (right HG, both p<0.001; right STG, both p<0.001; right INS, both p=0.003; right PrG, p=0.029 and 0.016, respectively; right PoG, p=0.025 and 0.010, respectively; right MTG, p=0.010 and 0.005, respectively; all with Bonferroni correction), reflecting robust auditory neural representations of the 4 Hz sequence of sound stimuli.
evidence: Supported by post hoc comparisons with Bonferroni correction.

claim: The activation observed at 4 Hz under the imagery and baseline conditions was stronger than that observed at 0.8 Hz under the imagery condition in the right INS.
source: In the right hemisphere, the activation observed at 4 Hz under the imagery and baseline conditions was stronger than that observed at 0.8 Hz under the imagery condition in most regions (right HG, both p<0.001; right STG, both p<0.001; right INS, both p=0.003; right PrG, p=0.029 and 0.016, respectively; right PoG, p=0.025 and 0.010, respectively; right MTG, p=0.010 and 0.005, respectively; all with Bonferroni correction), reflecting robust auditory neural representations of the 4 Hz sequence of sound stimuli.
evidence: Supported by post hoc comparisons with Bonferroni correction.

claim: The activation observed at 4 Hz under the imagery and baseline conditions was stronger than that observed at 0.8 Hz under the imagery condition in the right PrG.
source: In the right hemisphere, the activation observed at 4 Hz under the imagery and baseline conditions was stronger than that observed at 0.8 Hz under the imagery condition in most regions (right HG, both p<0.001; right STG, both p<0.001; right INS, both p=0.003; right PrG, p=0.029 and 0.016, respectively; right PoG, p=0.025 and 0.010, respectively; right MTG, p=0.010 and 0.005, respectively; all with Bonferroni correction), reflecting robust auditory neural representations of the 4 Hz sequence of sound stimuli.
evidence: Supported by post hoc comparisons with Bonferroni correction.

claim: The activation observed at 4 Hz under the imagery and baseline conditions was stronger than that observed at 0.8 Hz under the imagery condition in the right PoG.
source: In the right hemisphere, the activation observed at 4 Hz under the imagery and baseline conditions was stronger than that observed at 0.8 Hz under the imagery condition in most regions (right HG, both p<0.001; right STG, both p<0.001; right INS, both p=0.003; right PrG, p=0.029 and 0.016, respectively; right PoG, p=0.025 and 0.010, respectively; right MTG, p=0.010 and 0.005, respectively; all with Bonferroni correction), reflecting robust auditory neural representations of the 4 Hz sequence of sound stimuli.
evidence: Supported by post hoc comparisons with Bonferroni correction.

claim: The activation observed at 4 Hz under the imagery and baseline conditions was stronger than that observed at 0.8 Hz under the imagery condition in the right MTG.
source: In the right hemisphere, the activation observed at 4 Hz under the imagery and baseline conditions was stronger than that observed at 0.8 Hz under the imagery condition in most regions (right HG, both p<0.001; right STG, both p<0.001; right INS, both p=0.003; right PrG, p=0.029 and 0.016, respectively; right PoG, p=0.025 and 0.010, respectively; right MTG, p=0.010 and 0.005, respectively; all with Bonferroni correction), reflecting robust auditory neural representations of the 4 Hz sequence of sound stimuli.
evidence: Supported by post hoc comparisons with Bonferroni correction.

claim: No significant difference was observed in the brain activation levels at 4 Hz between the imagery condition and baseline condition, except in the right MFG.
source: No significant difference was observed in the brain activation levels at 4 Hz between the imagery condition and baseline condition, except in the right MFG, in which the activation at 4 Hz during mental imagery was stronger than that at baseline (p=0.014).
evidence: Supported by post hoc comparisons with Bonferroni correction.

claim: In the right MFG, the activation at 4 Hz during mental imagery was stronger than that at baseline.
source: No significant difference was observed in the brain activation levels at 4 Hz between the imagery condition and baseline condition, except in the right MFG, in which the activation at 4 Hz during mental imagery was stronger than that at baseline (p=0.014).
evidence: Supported by post hoc comparisons with Bonferroni correction and shown in Figure 4.

claim: The isolated neural networks underlying speech mental imagery involve the left central-frontal lobe, the left inferior occipital lobe and the right inferior parietal lobule, and these networks are disassociated from the sensory-driven processes.
source: These data indicate that the isolated neural networks underlying speech mental imagery involve the left central-frontal lobe, the left inferior occipital lobe and the right inferior parietal lobule, and that these networks are disassociated from the sensory-driven processes.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the MEG source estimation results.

claim: High gamma activity (60–100 Hz) in sEEG is highly correlated with the neural firing rate.
source: We analyzed the power of sEEG data in the high gamma band (60–100 Hz), which is highly correlated with the neural firing rate (Mukamel et al., 2011; Ray and Maunsell, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Mukamel et al., 2011 and Ray and Maunsell, 2011.

claim: Responsive contacts were found in five subjects with significant 4 Hz spectral peaks in the left posterior INS, left anterior SMG, bilateral middle STG, left HG and right middle MTG under the mental imagery and/or baseline conditions.
source: We found responsive contacts in five subjects with significant 4 Hz spectral peaks in the left posterior INS, left anterior SMG, bilateral middle STG, left HG and right middle MTG under the mental imagery and/or baseline conditions.
evidence: Supported by sEEG data analysis.

claim: Significant spectral responses at the imagery-rate frequency of 0.8 Hz were found when the participant was asked to perform a mental imagery task following the 4 Hz sound sequence.
source: Most importantly, we found significant spectral responses at the imagery-rate frequency of 0.8 Hz when the participant was asked to perform a mental imagery task following the 4 Hz sound sequence (t19 = 3.61, p=0.021, Cohen's d = 0.81, paired one-sided t test, FDR corrected) (Figure 5a).
evidence: Supported by sEEG data analysis and shown in Figure 5a.

claim: The imagery-responsive contact was localized in the operIFG, which is consistent with the MEG source results in the Montreal Neurological Institute (MNI) space.
source: The imagery-responsive contact was localized in the operIFG, which is consistent with the MEG source results in the Montreal Neurological Institute (MNI) space (Figure 5b).
evidence: Supported by sEEG localization analysis and shown in Figure 5b.

claim: Under the mental imagery condition, the averaged time course of the high gamma activity in the operIFG periodically changed every 1.25 s (0.8 Hz), with an increasing amplitude near the last number of each mentally constructed group.
source: Unlike in the baseline condition, under the mental imagery condition, the averaged time course of the high gamma activity in the operIFG periodically changed every 1.25 s (0.8 Hz), with an increasing amplitude near the last number of each mentally constructed group (Figure 5c).
evidence: Supported by sEEG time course analysis and shown in Figure 5c.

claim: Significant spectral responses at the stimulus-rate frequency of 4 Hz were found in the left posterior INS, anterior SMG and HG under the mental imagery condition.
source: In the left hemisphere, significant 4 Hz peaks were observed at the contacts localized in the posterior INS, anterior SMG and HG under the mental imagery condition and at the contacts localized in the middle STG, posterior INS, anterior SMG and HG under the baseline condition.
evidence: Supported by sEEG data analysis.

claim: Significant spectral responses at the stimulus-rate frequency of 4 Hz were found in the left middle STG, posterior INS, anterior SMG and HG under the baseline condition.
source: In the left hemisphere, significant 4 Hz peaks were observed at the contacts localized in the posterior INS, anterior SMG and HG under the mental imagery condition and at the contacts localized in the middle STG, posterior INS, anterior SMG and HG under the baseline condition.
evidence: Supported by sEEG data analysis.

claim: Significant spectral responses at 4 Hz were found in the right middle STG under the baseline condition and the mental imagery condition.
source: Specifically, the right middle STG was responsive to the 4 Hz stimuli under the baseline condition and the mental imagery condition.
evidence: Supported by sEEG data analysis.

claim: The right middle MTG was responsive to the 4 Hz stimuli only under the baseline condition.
source: The right middle MTG was responsive to the 4 Hz stimuli only under the baseline condition.
evidence: Supported by sEEG data analysis.

claim: Brain regions with significant spectral peaks at 4 Hz in sEEG mainly agreed with the estimated neural sources based on the MEG data.
source: These brain regions with significant spectral peaks at 4 Hz mainly agreed with the estimated neural sources based on the MEG data (Table 1).
evidence: This is a comparison between sEEG and MEG results.

claim: The 4 Hz peaks were significantly larger than zero under the baseline condition in the left posterior INS.
source: The one-tailed paired t tests revealed significant 4 Hz peak powers under the baseline condition in several brain areas, including the left posterior INS (t19 = 24.82, p<0.001, Cohen's d = 3.05), left anterior SMG (t58 = 2.32, p=0.012, Cohen's d = 0.30), left HG (t99 = 10.10, p<0.001, Cohen's d = 1.07), bilateral middle STG (left, t19 = 8.60, p<0.001, Cohen's d = 1.92; right, t99 = 9.28, p<0.001, Cohen's d = 0.93) and right middle MTG (t18 = 4.59, p<0.001, Cohen's d = 1.05).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of sEEG data and shown in Figure 5g.

claim: The 4 Hz peaks were significantly larger than zero under the baseline condition in the left anterior SMG.
source: The one-tailed paired t tests revealed significant 4 Hz peak powers under the baseline condition in several brain areas, including the left posterior INS (t19 = 24.82, p<0.001, Cohen's d = 3.05), left anterior SMG (t58 = 2.32, p=0.012, Cohen's d = 0.30), left HG (t99 = 10.10, p<0.001, Cohen's d = 1.07), bilateral middle STG (left, t19 = 8.60, p<0.001, Cohen's d = 1.92; right, t99 = 9.28, p<0.001, Cohen's d = 0.93) and right middle MTG (t18 = 4.59, p<0.001, Cohen's d = 1.05).
